claims.text: NbTaTiV and CrMoNbV are refractory BCC high-entropy alloys relevant to the proposed comparison.
The proposed baseline compositions have low lattice misfit.
Increasing lattice misfit creates stronger local elastic fields.
Stronger local elastic fields preferentially impede edge-dislocation glide.
Edge dislocations in some complex BCC HEAs encounter large glide-energy barriers.
Increasing lattice misfit shifts plasticity from screw-dislocation-dominated to edge-dislocation-dominated behavior.
Plastic deformation in NbTaTiV and CrMoNbV can be controlled by edge dislocations.
Plastic flow in conventional BCC elemental metals and dilute alloys is generally controlled by screw dislocations.
A transition to edge-dislocation-controlled plasticity raises the critical resolved shear stress.
Large barriers to edge-dislocation glide can produce high strength and high-temperature strength retention in refractory BCC HEAs.
Higher lattice misfit will produce greater yield strength than a low-misfit baseline.
Higher lattice misfit will produce greater hardness than a low-misfit baseline.
Low-misfit refractory BCC HEAs are predominantly screw-dislocation controlled and therefore have lower hardness and yield strength.
Composition can be varied through controlled casting or powder metallurgy and homogenization to create a low-to-high lattice-misfit series while retaining a single-phase microstructure.
In situ neutron diffraction and high-resolution TEM can be used together to establish edge-dislocation-dominated deformation in refractory BCC HEAs.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloy remains single phase and thermal activation does not override dislocation-core effects.
Phase transformations or significant solute clustering can place an alloy outside the proposed mechanism's valid regime.
A simultaneous absence of a statistically significant increase in edge-dislocation population and of enhanced hardness or yield strength with increasing misfit would falsify the proposed mechanism.
